title: Start here
summary: Three repositories, one data contract and the order in which to set them up.
text: Start here How to set up a decompilation repository that builds in a private environment, accepts reviewed contributions and publishes its progress to this site. This guide is written for someone, or some agent, dropped into an empty repository with a game binary and no other context. Followed in order, it ends with a repository whose every push to main builds each target, verifies it byte for byte, measures it with objdiff and publishes the measurement to the progress site. The only things it cannot decide for you are your project's parameters: the platform, the compiler versions and tooling, the split configuration, the target ids and the presentation. Everything else is specified exactly, every command, file name, field and secret named here matches the shipped code, and a scaffold check in CI keeps the repository matching the guide afterwards. The three repositories Each game is three repositories. Two are yours; the third is shared by every game on the site. Repository Visibility Holds owner/game public Source, headers, target configuration, tools and CI. The only place contributors work. owner/game-build private The original executables and the toolchain, built into a container image on GitHub Container Registry. Also private. mitsevox/decomp-data public, shared The published measurements of every game, served by GitHub Pages at https://mitsevox.github.io/decomp-data/ . The site itself, mitsevox/mitsevox.github.io , is a static page that reads the data repository at view time. It also hosts the publish action, the scaffold check, the starter kit, the scaffold spec, the repository settings standard and the data contract. Adding a game changes nothing in the site repository. owner/game (public) owner/game-build (private) push to main push to main validate.yml image.yml plan: which targets changed docker build: /orig/<target>/..., toolchain tests: tool tests, scaffold check push ghcr.io/owner/game-build:main, print digest Validate <target>, inside the image <--- referenced by digest copy the original configure, build, check the executable hash objdiff report -> build/<target>/report.json publish action (main only) -----------> mitsevox/decomp-data (public) data/game/<target>/latest.json, history.json, map.json data/game/game.json, index.json deploy.yml -> GitHub Pages ^ mitsevox.github.io/games/game/ reads /decomp-data/ at view time Placeholders used throughout Placeholder Stands for owner/game your public source repository owner/game-build your private build-image repository OWNER_LOGIN the owner's GitHub login game the game's slug on the site, [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]* GAME01-rev0 a target id, [A-Za-z0-9._-]+ ; GAME01 is its label, 0 its revision VERSION_GAME01_REV0 that target's preprocessor define, derived from the id ghcr.io/owner/game-build@sha256:... the build image, always referenced by digest DATA_APP_CLIENT_ID , DATA_APP_PRIVATE_KEY the repository variable and the publish environment secret that hold the publishing credential The examples are for a GameCube target built with decomp-toolkit and dtk-template, because that is what the reference repositories use. Another platform changes the toolchain, the original's path inside the image and the build commands; it changes nothing in the layout, the CI structure, publishing or the site. The setup path Repository layout : create the public repository with the tracked and ignored paths and the root allowlist. Targets : write config/targets.json , config/site.json and config/ci-targets.json ; scaffold config/<id>/ with tools/new_target.py . Build environment : create the private repository, build the image, make the package readable by the public repository, note the digest. Build, verify, measure : get a byte-identical relink locally and an objdiff report.json ; learn how version differences are written and read. Evidence and the contribution workflow : adopt AGENTS.md , CONTRIBUTING.md and the PR template. CI : install validate.yml with your image digest and build commands; the scaffold check runs in it. Publishing : create the GitHub App credential, add the variable and the publish environment with its secret, push to main . Repository settings : apply the settings standard to both repositories. The site : check the page, commit cover art to the data repository. Data contract describes what the publish action writes; Troubleshooting lists the failure messages; Starter kit is the download with every copyable file and the scaffold spec. What done looks like A push to main runs Validate with the jobs Plan affected targets , Tool tests , Validate <target id> for each affected active target and Validate targets . The Tool tests job's Check the scaffold step reports no warnings. The Validate <target id> job ends with Publish to the site , and the data repository gains a commit titled game GAME01-rev0: <sha>, <n>% code linked . The data repository's Deploy workflow runs, and https://mitsevox.github.io/games/game/ shows the new measurement within a few minutes. A pull request runs the same build, checks that the report converts and skips the publish step; it cannot merge until Validate targets passes and the owner merges it. python3 tools/repo_settings.py --repo owner/game --check reports no drift. Glossary Term Meaning target One original binary the project matches: a game id plus a disc revision, region or platform. Identified by a stable id. active A target that is built, verified and measured. planned and archived targets are listed on the page but never built. define VERSION_<ID> : the id upper-cased with - and . replaced by _ . The preprocessor symbol under which a target's differences live. group A macro in include/version.h naming two or more targets that share a difference, such as a region. original The unmodified executable, kept in the private image and never in the public repository. build image The private container image with the originals and the toolchain, referenced by digest. objdiff report report.json , written by objdiff-cli report generate ; the only measurement input the publish action reads. linked Bytes of units that compile from source into the byte-identical executable ( Matching objects). matched Bytes that match exactly whether linked or not (exact functions in NonMatching units count). fuzzy Size-weighted similarity of every function and data section. tier A, B or C: what a PR touches decides which review records it needs. review record A PR comment that starts with Revision: , Targets: and an Accuracy: or Hostile: verdict. scaffold check The composite action in the site repository that compares a checkout with the kit and the spec, in warn mode. publish action mitsevox/mitsevox.github.io/.github/actions/publish , which converts the report into the contract files and pushes them. data repository mitsevox/decomp-data : one directory per game and target, served by Pages. contract The schema-1 file format ( contract/README.md ); publish.py check is its executable form. Using this guide with an agent Give the agent the whole guide as one Markdown file , the starter archive and the project parameters. The starter kit has a prompt. An agent cannot obtain the original, create the private repository, install the GitHub App or set repository settings on its own; the guide marks those steps as the owner's.

title: Repository layout
summary: What the public repository tracks, what it ignores and where each file lives.
text: Repository layout What the public repository tracks, what it ignores and where each file lives. The public repository This is the layout of a GameCube or Wii project built with dtk-template , with the files the starter kit provides marked. Keep the names: the CI workflow, the tools, the scaffold check and the publish action refer to them. game/ README.md targets, owner, build commands; seven fixed headings CONTRIBUTING.md tiers, task loop, matching integrity, checklist (starter) AGENTS.md fixed header, then the project's own section (starter) CLAUDE.md one line: @AGENTS.md (starter) CREDITS.md origin and license of imported source (starter) .gitignore, .gitattributes originals, generated output; LF for toolkit files (starter) configure.py build configuration: libraries, objects, flags (dtk-template) config/ targets.json the target list, schema 1 (starter) site.json presentation on the site (starter) ci-targets.json which shared paths affect every target (starter) README.md evidence record format (starter) GAME01-rev0/ one directory per target, named by its id config.yml decomp-toolkit project: original path, hash, symbols, splits splits.txt, symbols.txt toolkit inputs build.sha1 expected hash of the built executable evidence.tsv curated claims README.md the target in one paragraph src/ reconstructed source, shared by every target include/ version.h the version-difference rule and group macros (starter) tools/ __init__.py (starter) targets.py reads config/targets.json, derives the define (starter) ci_targets.py selects affected targets in CI (starter) versions.py view, diff and check version differences (starter) evidence.py checks evidence.tsv (starter) new_target.py scaffolds config/<id>/ (starter) matching_scope.py shows and pins what each unit claims to link on (starter) measuring_tools.py lists tool versions for provenance, verifies them (starter) tier.py the review tier a diff needs, checked in CI (starter) credits.py the credits a merge will publish, checked in CI (starter) project.py, ninja_syntax.py, download_tool.py, ... dtk-template tests/ test_targets.py (starter) docs/ durable project knowledge references/ text only, regenerable by a named tool, no file over 4 MB licenses/ license texts of imported source orig/GAME01-rev0/.gitkeep where the original goes locally; the file itself is ignored build/ generated, ignored .github/ workflows/validate.yml (starter) pull_request_template.md (starter) Three directories are keyed by the target id and nothing else: config/<target id>/ for inputs, orig/<target id>/ for the original, build/<target id>/ for everything generated, including build.ninja , objdiff.json and report.json . Switching targets never overwrites another target's files. This holds for a project with a single target too: there is no flat, unkeyed layout to grow out of later. Shared and per target A file is per target only when it holds an address, a hash or a unit list of one binary: config/<id>/config.yml , splits.txt , symbols.txt , build.sha1 , evidence.tsv , README.md , an ldscript.tpl when the toolkit needs one, and tool reports. Everything else has one copy: src/ , include/ , configure.py listing the union of units, tools/ , tests/ , docs/ , references/ and the three JSON files under config/ . A unit that exists on some targets only is simply absent from the other targets' splits.txt ; there is no per-target source file and no unit-to-target table. Version differences inside a shared file are #if VERSION_<ID> blocks, described in Build, verify, measure . The root allowlist The root holds the required files plus these directories and nothing else: src/ , include/ , extern/ (verbatim imported source trees, each with its own credits), tools/ , tests/ , docs/ , references/ , licenses/ , orig/ , build/ , config/ , .github/ , .vscode/ , and the files LICENSE , CLAUDE.md and .flake8 . Anything else at the root is a warning from the scaffold check; project material goes under docs/ , tools/ or references/ . Two things never exist: a copy of upstream toolkit documentation under docs/dtk/ , and config/<id>/config.example.yml ; link dtk-template at its pinned revision from the README instead. Tracked and ignored Public Git holds reviewed source, headers, tools, curated evidence and configuration. It never holds: original executables, disc images or extracted assets ( orig/*/* is ignored; orig/<target id>/.gitkeep marks the directory); generated objects, build directories, objdiff and editor configuration ( build/ , build.ninja , objdiff.json , compile_commands.json ); complete debug exports, private analysis databases or discarded trial variants. The starter .gitignore covers these for a dtk-template project; the scaffold check requires it to cover orig/*/* , build/ , *.dol and *.elf at least. A .gitignore entry does not remove a file already tracked; inspect git status before every commit that touches orig/ . The private repository game-build/ Dockerfile originals + toolchain into one image (starter) .github/workflows/image.yml builds, verifies and publishes the image (starter) README.md (starter) orig/GAME01-rev0/main.dol the original, committed here The private repository is the only place the original is stored. It is committed there because the image build copies it in and checks its hash; see Build environment . The data repository You do not create this one; the publish action writes into it. For reference, it looks like this after the first publish of game : decomp-data/ index.json {"schema": 1, "games": ["game", ...]} .nojekyll .github/workflows/deploy.yml Pages deploy on every push data/game/game.json presentation and the target list data/game/cover.webp optional, committed by hand data/game/GAME01-rev0/latest.json data/game/GAME01-rev0/history.json data/game/GAME01-rev0/map.json Only active targets have a directory. See Data contract . Naming Target ids are [A-Za-z0-9._-]+ and stable forever: they name directories, the site's ?target= value and the data directory. The convention is <label>-rev<N> for discs with a game id ( GAME01-rev0 ) and <serial>-v<version> where the platform carries a serial and a version ( SLUS-20349-v1.01 ). A target's define is VERSION_<ID> with the id upper-cased and - and . replaced by _ : GAME01-rev0 gives VERSION_GAME01_REV0 , SLUS-20349-v1.01 gives VERSION_SLUS_20349_V1_01 . tools/targets.py define <id> prints it; nothing stores it. The slug is [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]* and names the game on the site: /games/<slug>/ and data/<slug>/ . Unit names are source paths. Unknown functions keep tool-generated address labels ( fn_<hex> with decomp-toolkit, func_<hex> with splat). The publish action counts a function as named only when its symbol is not such a label, so a descriptive name is a claim and needs evidence. Files under src/ use recovered paths when established; a descriptive file name counts as named while its boundaries remain provisional. Branch names are free. The aggregate CI check is always named Validate targets .

title: Targets
summary: config/targets.json, config/site.json and config/ci-targets.json, field by field.
text: Targets config/targets.json , config/site.json and config/ci-targets.json , field by field, and what adding a target takes. A target is one original binary. A game with one disc revision has one target; a second revision, region or platform is a second entry, never a replacement. Lay out every project as multi-target from the first commit, even with one disc. The target id always carries its revision ( GAME01-rev0 , never a bare GAME01 ), every per-target path is keyed by that id, and targets.json is a list with one entry. Adding a revision or region later is then a new folder and a new list entry; nothing is renamed or moved. A target id is permanent once published, because it names the target's directory in the data repository and the ?target= value in its URLs. The three files below are the producer's only inputs to the site apart from the objdiff report. Copies with placeholders are in the starter kit . config/targets.json { "schema": 1, "defaultTarget": "GAME01-rev0", "targets": [ {"id": "GAME01-rev0", "platform": "gamecube", "label": "GAME01", "region": "USA", "revision": "0", "sha1": "0000000000000000000000000000000000000000", "status": "active"}, {"id": "GAME01-rev1", "platform": "gamecube", "label": "GAME01", "region": "USA", "revision": "1", "sha1": "1111111111111111111111111111111111111111", "status": "planned"} ] } Field Meaning Rule schema Format version Always 1 defaultTarget The target the game page and hub card show first Must be listed, and must be active id The target's identity: directory names, ?target= , the data directory, the define [A-Za-z0-9._-]+ , unique, never changed once published; no two ids may give the same define platform Lower-case platform name [a-z0-9]+ , for example gamecube , wii , ps2 label Display: the game id on disc; the target picker groups by it Non-empty string region Display Non-empty string revision Display: the disc revision, unrelated to Git revisions; the picker groups by it under label Non-empty string sha1 SHA-1 of the original executable 40 lower-case hex digits status active : built, verified, measured, published. planned or archived : listed on the page, never built One of the three Two readers validate this file and both must accept it. tools/targets.py (starter) rejects any other field, requires exactly schema , defaultTarget and targets at the top level, and requires defaultTarget to be active. The publish action's publish.py reads the seven fields above, requires the default to be listed and writes the list verbatim into game.json . Run python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_*.py' after every edit: tests/test_targets.py loads the file. tools/targets.py is the one reader of this file in the repository: configure.py takes its version list from it, the CI planner derives each target's paths from it, and python3 tools/targets.py check confirms that the three places a hash lives agree per target ( targets.json , config/<id>/config.yml and config/<id>/build.sha1 ) and that every target has its files. The Tool tests job runs it. What active requires An active target has an entry here with the original's SHA-1; config/<id>/ with the toolkit inputs ( config.yml , splits.txt , symbols.txt for decomp-toolkit), build.sha1 , evidence.tsv and README.md ; orig/<id>/.gitkeep ; the original in the private image at /orig/<id>/<original path> ; and a byte-identical relink proven by CI. Progress is not a condition: a target at a true 0 percent, every unit NonMatching , is active. A planned or archived target needs config/<id>/README.md and orig/<id>/.gitkeep only. To find the SHA-1 of an original: sha1sum /path/to/main.dol # Linux shasum -a 1 /path/to/main.dol # macOS config/site.json { "schema": 1, "slug": "game", "title": "A Game: Full Title", "shortTitle": "A Game", "console": "GameCube", "year": "2002", "contributions": {"accepting": false}, "contributors": false, "artwork": {"cover": "cover.webp", "width": 1112, "height": 1600} } Field Meaning Rule schema Format version 1 slug The game's name everywhere on the site and in the data repository [a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]* , required title Full title shown on the page Required, non-empty shortTitle Shorter title for the hub card Optional; defaults to title console Display name of the console; the hub filters by it and it picks the console icon Required, non-empty year Release year, a string Optional contributions {"accepting": true, "guideUrl": "<url>"} shows a Contribute link to that URL; accepting: false hides it Optional; defaults to {"accepting": false} contributors true publishes who made each exact function exact and shows the rankings ( Publishing , "Credits") Optional; defaults to false artwork cover is a file name relative to data/<slug>/ in the data repository, width and height its pixel size Optional; add it only after committing the cover ( The site ) The publish action copies this file into game.json on every publish, adding repository (from the CI run's GITHUB_REPOSITORY ), defaultTarget and targets . Changing the presentation is therefore an edit to this file followed by a merge to main ; the next publish of any active target rewrites game.json . config/ci-targets.json { "schemaVersion": 1, "shared": ["src/**", "include/**", "asm/**", "configure.py", "tools/**", ".github/workflows/validate.yml", "config/targets.json", "config/ci-targets.json", "config/site.json"], "nonBuild": ["*.md", "docs/**", "references/**", "tests/**", ".github/pull_request_template.md", ".gitignore", ".gitattributes"] } tools/ci_targets.py reads it in the Plan affected targets job and decides which active targets a push or pull request must build: A changed path that matches Selects a shared pattern every active target config/<id>/** or orig/<id>/** that target, if active a nonBuild pattern only nothing no pattern at all every active target (unknown paths never skip validation) The per-target patterns are not written down: every target owns config/<id>/** and orig/<id>/** , and the planner derives them from targets.json , so adding a target never touches this file. Patterns are fnmatch globs matched against the repository-relative path; * and ** both match across / . Rules: schemaVersion is 1 ; the keys are exactly schemaVersion , shared and nonBuild (a targets key is a scaffold-check warning); no pattern may start with / or contain .. . A manual run ( workflow_dispatch ) and a push with no known base (first push, force push) select every active target, and so does a changed path that matches no pattern. A change that selects no target still runs the Tool tests job and passes the Validate targets check. tests/** is nonBuild in the kit because every test runs in Tool tests on the bare runner; a repository whose tests need the toolchain and run in the target job's Project checks lists tests/** under shared instead, so that a test change rebuilds every target ( CI , builds without configure.py ). Adding a target Hash the executable and add a planned entry to config/targets.json . Commit the original to the private repository under orig/<id>/ , add its COPY and checksum lines to the Dockerfile and the image.yml verification, push, and take the new digest ( Build environment ). By hand; minutes. python3 tools/new_target.py <id> writes config/<id>/config.yml with the original's path and hash from the registry, an empty evidence.tsv with its header row, a README.md stub and orig/<id>/.gitkeep . It refuses an id the registry does not list and never overwrites a file: a file that already exists is adopted, and left as it is, only when it is exactly the stub the tool would write, an empty .gitkeep , or the README.md that is a planned or archived target's only file; that placeholder is kept with a printed reminder to rewrite it, since it describes a target that is not built, and anything else stops the tool. python3 tools/matching_scope.py pin <every id active so far> rewrites every unconditional Matching in configure.py to MatchingFor(<those ids>) , so that the new target inherits no claim: on it every unit is NonMatching until proven. It must name every active target, all of them (a subset would drop the others' claims), and the new target is still planned or archived at this point. For the targets named nothing changes: run python3 configure.py --version <id> for each and compare the build.ninja and objdiff.json it writes (under build/<id>/ , or at the repository root with stock dtk-template, where the next configure overwrites them) with the ones from before the rewrite: identical; objdiff.json needs the original at hand. The file is read as Python tokens; an Object call whose first argument is none of Matching , NonMatching , Equivalent or MatchingFor , or a use of Matching anywhere else, stops the tool and is pinned by hand. python3 tools/matching_scope.py show lists each unit's declared scope. Run the toolkit's analysis on the new original for a first symbols.txt and splits.txt , build, and confirm that the relink is byte-identical with every unit NonMatching on the new target. Write config/<id>/build.sha1 , set status: active , and point validate.yml at the new digest. Hand-driven; hours. Push to main . The planner builds the new target because config/<id>/ changed, and the first main run publishes it: data/<slug>/<id>/ appears in the data repository. Then widen the shared work: a function already decompiled for a sibling counts on the new target as soon as the new target's splits.txt names the same unit, configure.py says Matching or MatchingFor for it there, and its symbols.txt gives the function the same name. Nothing is copied between targets; each target's own objdiff report scores it. Seeding symbols.txt and splits.txt from the sibling is the real cost of a new revision; a symbol-porting tool belongs here once a second original has passed step 4. Setting a published target to archived keeps its data directory and history in the data repository, but the site reads latest.json only for active targets, so the page lists it without a measurement. Removing a target from the list entirely removes it from game.json on the next publish; the data directory is deleted by hand, if at all.

title: Build environment
summary: The private image that holds the originals and the toolchain, pinned by digest.
text: Build environment The private image that holds the originals and the toolchain, pinned by digest. CI must build with the original executable, and the original must never be public. The solution is a second, private repository whose only job is to build a container image containing the original and the exact toolchain, and to publish that image to GitHub Container Registry as a private package that the public repository's workflow may pull. The public repository then references the image by digest, so every build runs against a known set of bytes. The private repository Create owner/game-build as a private repository. Copy the three files from the starter kit's build-image/ directory to its root and commit the original under orig/<target id>/ : game-build/ Dockerfile .github/workflows/image.yml README.md orig/GAME01-rev0/main.dol The original is committed to this repository on purpose: the image build copies it in and verifies its SHA-1, so the image can only be produced from the right file. The Dockerfile The starter Dockerfile is a three-stage build for a GameCube or Wii project: dependencies : downloads the binutils and compiler archives, checks their SHA-256 and unpacks them to /binutils and /compilers . dtk : clones decomp-toolkit at the tag configure.py pins, checks the commit and builds it to /dtk . A project patch to the toolkit is applied in this stage. The final image: copies every original to /orig/<target id>/<original path> , checks each SHA-1 against the value you also put in config/targets.json , copies the tools in, and installs gcompat git ninja python3 . Parameters, each marked PARAMETER in the file: the archive URLs and checksums, the toolkit tag and commit, and one COPY plus one sha1sum -c line per active target. The base images are pinned by digest; keep them that way. What the final image must provide, whatever the platform, because validate.yml and the publish action run inside it: Requirement Why /orig/<target id>/<original path> for every active target The Provide target original step copies it into the checkout sh , git , python3 Composite action steps run with sh ; tools/ and publish.py are Python; publish.py runs git log , git clone and git push gcompat on Alpine The Actions runner mounts its own glibc Node.js into the container to run actions/checkout and the token-minting action The toolchain at fixed paths The configure command in validate.yml names them ( /usr/local/bin/dtk , /binutils , /compilers in the starter) The image workflow image.yml runs on every push and pull request: Build image : docker build --tag ghcr.io/owner/game-build:candidate . Verify toolchain inside image : runs sha1sum on each original and probes the tool files. Edit this step to match your Dockerfile ( PARAMETER ). Publish image , on main only: logs in to ghcr.io with the workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN , pushes the tags :main and :<commit sha> , and appends the image digest ( ghcr.io/owner/game-build@sha256:... ) to the run summary. The job has packages: write ; nothing else in either repository does. Owner setup after the first publish These steps are done once, on GitHub, by the owner: Open the package game-build under the owner's packages and confirm its visibility is private . A package created by a workflow from a private repository starts private; check anyway. In the package settings, under Manage Actions access , add the repository owner/game with the Read role. This is what lets the public repository's workflow pull the image with its own GITHUB_TOKEN . Copy the digest from the Publish image step summary into validate.yml (the BUILD_IMAGE variable). The public workflow's target job declares permissions: packages: read and pulls with credentials: {username: github.actor, password: secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN} . No personal token is involved. Referencing the image by digest validate.yml names the image once, as BUILD_IMAGE: ghcr.io/owner/game-build@sha256:<64 hex digits> , never :main ; the target job runs in it and the variable is exported to every step. The digest is part of the measurement's provenance: tools/measuring_tools.py reads BUILD_IMAGE and the publish action records it as the build-environment tool in latest.json . The scaffold check warns on an image referenced by tag. Changing the digest is a reviewed change to validate.yml , and it is an owner decision: the image defines the compiler and the original, so a different image can change every number. Keep the digest line commented with the image workflow run that produced it. Pulling :main in validate.yml is never acceptable, and no bot bumps the digest. Two later conveniences have known triggers and are not built before them: a small tool that reads the image run summary and rewrites the digest line, once the third bump has been done by hand; and a shared toolchain base image with each game's image adding only /orig/<id>/ , once two repositories build on the same compiler pack. Other platforms The pattern does not depend on the platform. For another console, the Dockerfile's dependencies stage fetches that platform's toolchain, the original goes under /orig/<target id>/ at whatever path your build expects ( PARAMETER 2 in validate.yml and the toolchain's own configuration name it), and the configure and build commands in validate.yml change. A single image may hold several targets, and a reference binary from another platform may be added for comparison in the same way; it is just one more COPY with a checksum. Local builds Contributors build locally with their own copy of the game and their own tool installation; the image is for CI. Running the image locally is possible with docker run --rm -it -v "$PWD:/work" -w /work ghcr.io/owner/game-build@sha256:... sh after docker login ghcr.io , but only for people who already hold the original, because pulling the image requires read access to the private package.

title: Build, verify, measure
summary: Relink the original byte for byte, replace units with source and produce objdiff's report.
text: Build, verify, measure Relink the original byte for byte, replace units with source and produce objdiff's report. Three things happen in one ninja invocation, locally and in CI: the original is split into objects and relinked, the objects marked Matching are replaced by compiled source and the result is checked against the expected hash, and objdiff measures every unit against its original. The publish action reads only the last step's output, build/<target id>/report.json . The commands below are for decomp-toolkit and dtk-template, which the reference repositories use for GameCube. The section at the end says what another platform must provide instead. Local setup for a dtk-template project Start from dtk-template ( configure.py , tools/project.py and the rest of its tools/ ). dtk-template names its config folder after the game ID ( config/GAMEID/ ); rename it to the target id ( config/GAME01-rev0/ ) before adding anything, and use the target id wherever the template says version. Follow its documentation for config/<target id>/config.yml , splits.txt and symbols.txt ; those are the platform-specific part this guide cannot write for you. Record the template's revision in CREDITS.md and link its documentation from the README rather than copying it into the repository. Wire configure.py to the target list so the active targets are the only versions it accepts, --version takes a target id and the target's define is derived. Replace dtk-template's hard-coded VERSIONS list with: ```python from tools.targets import registry, build_targets, define TARGET_REGISTRY = registry() VERSIONS = build_targets(TARGET_REGISTRY) DEFAULT_VERSION = VERSIONS.index(TARGET_REGISTRY['defaultTarget']) ``` add Path("config/targets.json") and Path("tools/targets.py") to config.reconfig_deps , point config.config_path and config.check_sha_path at config/<version>/config.yml and config/<version>/build.sha1 , and pass f"-D{define(config.version)}" in cflags_base next to the template's -DBUILD_VERSION= . Remove type=str.upper from the --version argument: dtk-template upper-cases it, which no target id with a lower-case revision ( GAME01-rev0 ) can pass. dtk-template compiles each version into build/<version>/ and writes report.json there, but its tools/project.py writes build.ninja , objdiff.json and compile_commands.json at the repository root, and the next configure.py run overwrites them. The kit's validate.yml and README expect them under build/<target id>/ with everything else generated ( Repository layout ): either edit generate_build_ninja , generate_objdiff_config and generate_compile_commands in tools/project.py to write under config.build_dir / config.version , or keep the stock paths and write PARAMETER 3 and the README's build lines without -f ( ninja progress build/<id>/report.json ), configuring one target at a time. 3. Keep config.dtk_tag and config.objdiff_tag in configure.py as the single place tool versions are pinned; tools/measuring_tools.py reads them, and the Dockerfile builds the same dtk tag. The two can drift apart, since the build uses the image's dtk and not the tag; in CI tools/measuring_tools.py --verify runs the image's dtk --version and fails the job unless it reports the pinned tag, as a whole word. It verifies the version word only: a project that patches dtk and names the patch in the reported version (its hash, say) gets the stock version from the patched binary, so the patch itself is the image's to carry and the Dockerfile's to check. objdiff is downloaded at the pinned tag by the build itself, so the pin is what runs. 4. Place your own copy of the original at orig/<target id>/sys/main.dol , the path config.yml names ( orig/*/* is ignored by Git). The toolkit refuses an original whose hash differs from config.yml , and python3 tools/targets.py check confirms that config.yml , build.sha1 and targets.json agree. 5. Configure and build: sh python3 configure.py --version GAME01-rev0 ninja -f build/GAME01-rev0/build.ninja The generated build downloads dtk, objdiff and the compilers at their pinned tags unless --dtk , --objdiff and --compilers point at local copies. The build fails unless the linked executable's SHA-1 equals config/<target id>/build.sha1 , which must equal the original's hash from targets.json . Measure: sh ninja -f build/GAME01-rev0/build.ninja progress build/GAME01-rev0/report.json progress prints the per-category summary; build/<target id>/report.json is the objdiff report CI publishes. This is exactly the command the starter validate.yml runs, after the same configure.py call with the image's tool paths. With more than one active target, repeat steps 5 and 6 per target; the README's Building section shows the loop. A shared change is safe for every target only when every target has been built. What the three measures mean Each object in configure.py is declared Matching or NonMatching (dtk-template's Equivalent is for --non-matching builds and never counts). The publish action turns objdiff's report into the contract's three measures: Measure Source in the report What it says linked complete_code and complete_data : units whose metadata.complete is true, which dtk-template's generated objdiff.json sets for Matching objects Bytes that compile from source into the byte-identical executable matched matched_code and matched_data : functions at 100% and data sections at 100%, in any unit Bytes that match exactly, linked or not fuzzy size * fuzzy_match_percent / 100 summed over functions, and over data sections, by the action itself Size-weighted similarity So a NonMatching unit with three exact functions out of ten contributes those three functions' bytes to matched , their fuzzy score to fuzzy , and nothing to linked ; the original bytes stay linked. Promoting the unit to Matching moves its whole size into linked . Function counts come from the report too: exact is functions at 100%, named is functions whose symbol is not fn_<hex> or func_<hex> . File counts treat each unit as a file, named when the unit is not auto_generated and exact when it is named and both its code and data are fully matched. The action checks the report's own totals against its function list and refuses a report whose numbers disagree, so a report from an unexpected objdiff version fails the publish step rather than publishing wrong numbers. Pin config.objdiff_tag and change it deliberately. Partial source Useful partial reconstruction stays in its normal file under src/ and is registered as a NonMatching object. The combined executable still matches because the original bytes for that unit remain linked; objdiff measures the source separately. Reviewers and CI treat matching incompleteness as progress, not as a failure. See Contribution workflow for how partial units are reviewed and promoted. Version differences Every target has one preprocessor define, VERSION_<ID> : the id upper-cased with - and . replaced by _ , so GAME01-rev0 compiles with VERSION_GAME01_REV0 . tools/targets.py derives it and configure.py passes it; no file stores it. dtk-template also passes a numeric BUILD_VERSION ; it stays defined for compatibility and is never read, because BUILD_VERSION >= 1 stops meaning anything the day a region is inserted between two revisions. A difference lives in the shared file under #if VERSION_GAME01_REV0 . A condition is a boolean expression of VERSION_ tokens and group macros, with ! , && and || only, and nothing else: no numeric comparison, no other macro in the same condition. A version condition nested inside an ordinary #ifdef is fine; the two must not mix in one line. When two or more targets share a difference, name the group once in include/version.h : #define REGION_USA (VERSION_GAME01_REV0 || VERSION_GAME01_REV1) . The header exists from the first commit with the rule as its comment, so the first divergent PR cannot invent a second scheme. A condition names the targets it includes. The rule is exact: a branch is broad when a target listed later would take it, that is, when its condition holds with every VERSION_ token false ( #if !VERSION_GAME01_REV0 , #if !REGION_USA ), or when it is the #else of a chain none of whose conditions does. VERSION_GAME01_REV0 && !VERSION_GAME01_REV1 is not broad, and neither is a double negation through a group. With two targets listed a broad branch is the other target's and versions.py check only warns; from the third listed target on it is an error, so the pull request that lists a third target makes every such block explicit, with #elif VERSION_GAME01_REV1 or a group. view and diff resolve a broad branch like any other. Inline blocks are the default. When a function would carry three or more blocks, or more than about a third of its lines inside blocks, write the whole function once per variant under one function-level #if ... #else ... #endif , in the same file. Never a src/<id>/ file for a unit two targets share. A unit that matches on some targets only is Object(MatchingFor("GAME01-rev0"), "unit.cpp") ; a unit absent from a target is absent from that target's splits.txt . Compiler or flag differences between targets are whole profiles chosen by config.version in configure.py , with a compiler evidence row in each target's evidence.tsv . tools/versions.py reads this convention back: python3 tools/versions.py view --target GAME01-rev0 src/unit.cpp python3 tools/versions.py diff --target GAME01-rev0 --target GAME01-rev1 src/unit.cpp python3 tools/versions.py check view prints the file as one target compiles it: it resolves exactly the directives whose condition is a version expression and leaves every other directive and all macros untouched, so what you read is still source, not preprocessor output. diff is the unified diff between two targets' views; a reviewer of a change to a file with version blocks reads it instead of tracing the branches by eye. check fails on a VERSION_ token that is not a known define or group, a MatchingFor argument that is not a known target id, a version condition mixed with other macros, any BUILD_VERSION in src/ or include/ , and, once three targets are listed, a branch a later target would take (a printed warning while two are listed). The Tool tests job runs check ; the scaffold check runs it too. A function decompiled for one target counts for another automatically when, on that target, splits.txt names the unit, configure.py says Matching or MatchingFor for it, and symbols.txt gives the function the same name, because objdiff pairs by symbol name. Different addresses are a per-target symbols.txt and splits.txt matter and never touch source; a function present on one target only, or data that differs, is an #if block with MatchingFor until both targets link. Reading the report The publish action reads these parts of report.json , so any producer must write them the way objdiff does: Path in the report Use measures.total_code , matched_code , complete_code , total_data , matched_data , complete_data , total_functions , matched_functions The summary; 64-bit values are strings, zero values may be absent units[].name Unit name; the unit-prefix input (default main/ ) is stripped for display units[].metadata.complete , units[].metadata.auto_generated Linked status and tool-generated units units[].measures.total_data , matched_data , and matched_code , total_code Per-unit data tile and the exact-file test units[].sections[] : name , size , fuzzy_match_percent , metadata.virtual_address Section extents; sections named in code-sections (default .init,.text ) are code, all others data units[].functions[] : name , size , fuzzy_match_percent , metadata.virtual_address Function tiles and counts Every function must lie inside one of the code sections of its unit, or the action stops with <unit>: <function> lies outside the code sections . A platform whose code lives in differently named sections passes code-sections to the action ( Publishing ). Other platforms The per-target directory, the define rule, the planner, the tiers, the Targets table and the settings are toolchain-neutral. The publish action converts objdiff reports and nothing else, and objdiff supports several architectures, so a project on another platform that produces report.json with objdiff-cli report generate can use the whole pipeline unchanged apart from these parameters: the original's path under orig/<target id>/ ( PARAMETER 2 in validate.yml , the COPY in the Dockerfile, the toolchain's own config); the configure and build commands ( PARAMETER 3 in validate.yml ), which must fail unless the complete executable matches and must write build/<target id>/report.json ; config/<target id>/ holds a splat or custom configuration instead of dtk's three files; tools/versions.py reads the same #if convention, and the MatchingFor equivalent lives in whatever generates the build; the code-sections and unit-prefix inputs of the publish action and of the report check if the defaults do not fit; in tools/measuring_tools.py , TAGS (the version lines of configure.py to report) or PINS (the JSON pin files of a build without configure.py ), and VERIFY , the commands that confirm each image-installed tool's version against the pin. A producer that writes its own report sets a unit's metadata.complete only when the whole unit links from source into the byte-identical executable: that is what linked means on the site. A status of the producer's own, such as whether a unit's boundaries have evidence, stays in the repository's files; the contract has no field for it and it never sets complete . Bytes of a code section that no function covers (alignment padding, code the producer does not split into functions) become one (other code) tile per piece on the site, holding the matched bytes no exact function accounts for ( Data contract ). A project that cannot produce an objdiff report cannot use the publish action as shipped; that is a site-side change and outside this guide.

title: Evidence
summary: Recover what the target supports, record it, and never manufacture a match.
text: Evidence Recover what the target supports, record it, and never manufacture a match. A byte match proves that the compiler produced the same code from the submitted source; it proves nothing about names, types, intent or where the original source file boundaries were. The project's value is the evidence behind those claims, so the evidence is recorded in the repository next to the configuration it supports and is reviewed with it. Inventory before interpretation Inventory what the target and its references actually contain: the parsed filesystem, executables, symbols, debug information, linker maps, diagnostic strings, SDK references and related builds. Record hashes or revisions and which files were parsed. A claim that an artifact does not exist must say how thoroughly it was searched; a file-name search or a few strings is not enough. Related builds (another platform, another revision, another game on the same engine) suggest names and behavior. They do not prove the target's offsets, field widths, original names or source boundaries. Keep target evidence, reference evidence and inferred meaning separate. Reference material that agents read on every task lives under references/ : text only, regenerable by a named tool, no file over 4 MB. The scaffold check warns on anything larger. Bounded tasks Identify the functions, address ranges, candidate source unit, shared headers and dependencies before editing. Confirm accepted declarations on current main . Establish each function's full extent and the limits of any provisional unit; unresolved boundaries stay visible. For a field or signature, cite the actual loads and stores and the relevant caller or callee behavior. A nearby subsystem's access is not proof of the same layout. Preserve unknown offsets instead of inventing a convenient struct. The reconstruction loop Describe the behavior and the evidence-backed types before optimizing for a score. Write plausible source in the codebase's style. Compile with the documented unit or library profile. Compare the full function bytes, referenced data and relocations with objdiff. Investigate the remaining uncertainty, record the result and retain useful partial source. Uncertainty Useful investigation Behavior, references or ownership Target disassembly and bounded static analysis Different instruction selection or scheduling Controlled compiler experiments and the compiler's intermediate output Competing behavioral interpretations A bounded debugger or emulator trace with known inputs and conditions Candidate SDK or library reuse Fingerprints followed by calls, globals, types and boundary checks Record the tested revision, tool version and settings, inputs, conclusion and remaining uncertainty. Check decompiler output against instructions. Runtime observations establish what happened under those conditions, not the original source text. Keep bulk experiments private; retain concise reproducible evidence publicly. The evidence record Each target keeps config/<target id>/evidence.tsv , one claim per row, tab separated: kind start end subject origin start_boundary end_boundary evidence Column Values kind name , function , data , unit-anchor , unit , type , field , external , compiler , assembly , source-form , linker start , end Virtual addresses as 0x plus eight upper-case hex digits, end exclusive; - when unknown or inapplicable subject The symbol, source path, type or field concerned origin target (present in the target's bytes, symbols or debug information), signature (a named tool signature), related (another identified build), inferred (interpretation of the code) start_boundary , end_boundary exact , provisional , open or - , claimed independently of each other; anything but - only on function , data , unit , assembly and linker rows evidence A reproducible locator and what it establishes and leaves unknown Use separate rows for a name, a function extent, a field layout and a source-unit boundary: one claim never silently proves another. A name row with origin target needs explicit name evidence in the target; a name supported only by behavior is inferred . Compiler profiles are compiler rows at the unit or library level. The starter config/README.md is the full definition and goes into the repository as is. What earns a row A row is a claim a person or agent made that a reviewer must be able to challenge: an inferred name, a unit boundary, a type or field layout read from loads and stores, a compiler , source-form or linker claim. Tool output is not transcribed row by row. Symbol extents from the toolkit, debug names from a related build, signature hits from a library map: these are reproducible from references/ plus a tool at a pinned revision, so they get one row per tool run, with kind unit-anchor or name , origin related or signature , a subject that names the tool with its inputs and revision, and the regenerable report's path as the evidence. The table then stays readable in review, and the report is the evidence. python3 tools/evidence.py check runs in the Tool tests job and in the scaffold check: the header row, eight columns, the address format, the kinds and origins, edges only on the rows that have extents, non-empty subject and evidence. It checks form, not truth; the hostile checklist's Names row is the provenance check, and the publish action counts a function as named only when its symbol is not a tool label, so an unnamed function can never be published as named. Matching integrity Do not force a match through: per-function flags, optimization pragmas or compiler attributes introduced to force code generation; inline assembly, embedded instruction bytes or patched compiler output in place of compiled source; invented helpers, casts, volatile qualifiers, padding or control flow whose only justification is the bytes; altered symbol boundaries, excluded comparisons or progress categories that hide mismatches; behavioral changes made to satisfy the compiler. Compiler versions and flags need evidence at the compilation-unit or library level. A function-specific exception needs evidence that the original used it and the owner's explicit approval. Originally handwritten assembly needs provenance. Labeling a workaround a fake match does not make it acceptable; it stays a local experiment outside accepted source. When evidence runs out, keep the useful partial reconstruction as a NonMatching unit, keep the original bytes linked and record the gap. Partial similarity is progress; unsupported certainty is not. Imported and SDK code Retain the origin, source revision, license and local modifications of anything imported, in CREDITS.md and under licenses/ ; a verbatim imported tree goes under extern/ with its own credits. A fingerprint match is a candidate, especially for a short function; inspect target-specific calls, data ownership and compilation boundaries before importing. Imported code whose every name is target , signature or related is a tier B change: it gets the hostile review, not the blind accuracy pass. Comments in source explain intent, invariants and non-obvious relationships. Matching scores, compiler experiments, agent notes and review history belong in evidence.tsv or the PR, never in source comments.

title: Contribution workflow
summary: Review tiers sized to what a PR touches, draft PRs as reservations, independent records and an owner-only merge.
text: Contribution workflow Review tiers sized to what a PR touches, draft PRs as reservations, independent records and an owner-only merge. This is the contribution policy for a one-owner project where agents do most of the work. It is written for people and agents alike: the same rules, the same records, the same authority. The starter CONTRIBUTING.md states it in full and AGENTS.md summarizes it for agents; both go into the repository with the parameters filled in, and the scaffold check keeps their section headings and AGENTS.md 's header matching the kit. What protects matching integrity In order: CI proves that the complete executable of every affected target is byte-identical and measures each unit per target; the matching-integrity rules in CONTRIBUTING.md ; a reviewer who did not write the code reads reconstructed source against the disassembly and the evidence before an inferred name or boundary is published; the owner decides what merges. Everything else is proportionate to the risk a change carries. Authority Only the owner ( OWNER_LOGIN ) merges into main . Contributors and agents prepare branches, open PRs and review. A SHIP verdict and a green CI run are two different states, and neither lets a contributor merge. The authority is procedural for agents, which author under the owner's login, so a native approval rule would not tell an author from a reviewer; the main ruleset requires a pull request and the Validate targets check and nothing else, and the merges ruleset lets only the Repository admin role merge, so a contributor with write access cannot ( Repository settings ). Nobody but the owner changes branch rules, repository settings, the build image or its digest, or the access controls around them. A dependency problem is reported in an issue, not fixed by changing the dependency. Tiers The paths a PR touches decide what it needs before merge. The author states the tier in the PR's Scope line; CI's Check the declared tier step ( tools/tier.py ) fails a claim below what the diff needs, and the owner checks the rest. Tier Touches Required before merge A src/ or include/ with new or changed inferred names, types, fields or unit boundaries; splits.txt ; symbols.txt ; compiler profiles CI green, one blind accuracy record, one hostile record B src/ or include/ where every name and layout is target , signature or related (library imports, already-named code); promotions from NonMatching to Matching CI green, one hostile record C tools/ , tests/ , docs/ , references/ , workflows, config/*.json , root documents CI green The blind accuracy pass stays for tier A only: it is the one check that catches a wrong inferred name, and it reconciles nothing when the names come from an SDK or a sibling build. One task, start to finish Claim. Check open PRs and branches. Open a draft PR early with the unit names and target ids in its title; that is the reservation, and it ends when the PR closes. There is no expiry bookkeeping. Branch. Work on a dedicated branch from current main , in your own checkout or worktree: git switch -c your-task . Branches live in the repository, not in forks; CI refuses to build a fork's pull request because fork builds would otherwise reach the private image. Establish evidence. Boundaries, types and references before source; see Evidence . Search existing headers and accepted units before declaring a shared address. Reconstruct and measure. Compile and compare with objdiff. Keep discarded variants local. Register partial work as a NonMatching object in configure.py so CI measures it; promote to Matching when the unit links byte-identically. The source file does not move on promotion. A version difference goes under #if VERSION_<ID> in the shared file ( Build, verify, measure ). Record. Add evidence.tsv rows for every name, boundary, type and compiler claim in the same PR, to each affected target's file. Keep source comments free of scores and process notes. Check every target. Before calling a shared change safe for every target: build every active target and confirm build.sha1 on each; run objdiff per target for each touched unit; run python3 tools/versions.py diff on every file you added a block to and read the result; add the evidence rows per target. CI enforces the first two; the hostile checklist's Unit boundaries and Validation rows cover the rest. Fill the Targets table of the PR template from these results, one row per active target. Review. Tier A: a reviewer who did not author or shape the reconstruction interprets the scoped functions with the proposed names and comments withheld, reconciles that interpretation with the submission and posts an Accuracy: record; then a fresh reviewer applies the checklist in CONTRIBUTING.md (source fidelity, compiler settings, types and layouts, provenance and licence, names, comments, unit boundaries, comparison integrity, validation) and posts a Hostile: record with SHIP , FIX , REDO or BLOCKED . Tier B: the hostile record only. Tier C: none. Resolve and recheck. Fix findings; the reviewer rechecks the delta, not the whole PR, and posts a final-revision record that cites the earlier one. Submit. Fill the PR template: scope with the tier, the Targets table, evidence and validation, the records. Request the owner's decision only when CI and the records cover the final revision. Merge. The owner merges. On main , CI builds and publishes each affected target. Review records Each pass is one PR comment. The first line is the revision, the second the targets the record covers, the third the verdict; each header occurs once, outside quotes and code fences, so a record covering one target can never be read as covering both. Revision: FULL_COMMIT_SHA Targets: GAME01-rev0, GAME01-rev1 Accuracy: PASS Reviewer: identity and prior involvement Scope: functions, files and configuration checked Evidence: references and validation artifacts used Findings: results, uncertainties and resolutions Revision: FULL_COMMIT_SHA Targets: GAME01-rev0 Hostile: SHIP Reviewer: identity and prior involvement Checklist: PASS / FAIL / BLOCKED / justified N/A per category Findings: location, evidence and required correction Coverage: earlier records carried forward and delta checked Accepted values: Accuracy: PASS or Accuracy: N/A - <reason> (the reason is required), and Hostile: SHIP , FIX , REDO or BLOCKED . Nothing parses these comments; they are for the owner and the next reviewer to read, and the format exists so that they can be read at a glance. Reviewer independence Independence is about authorship and prior reasoning, not display names. A second agent spawned with the author's conversation is not independent; a reviewer given the task, the target evidence, the relevant configuration and the validation artifacts in a fresh context is. Each record states the reviewer's identity, prior involvement, supplied inputs and the reviewed revision. If isolation is impossible, disclose it; never assert an independent pass that did not occur. Partial source is reviewed for fidelity, evidence and comparison integrity. A measured mismatch is not a finding. A reviewer may return SHIP with documented incompleteness. Rechecks, refreshes and batches After a fix, the reviewer checks the finding, the correction and its affected dependencies and carries the rest of the coverage forward by linking the earlier record and its revision. A replacement reviewer may continue from that record. A full restart needs a concrete reason that invalidates coverage across the PR. After refreshing from main , verify the diff, conflict resolutions and shared declarations, then post final-revision records that cite the earlier ones and name the checked delta. An earlier verdict does not cover a new head. Compatible bounded contributions may be batched into one PR with each original PR, author revision and review coverage identified; the combined delta is reviewed and CI runs on the combined tree. Compiler-profile and comparison changes get their own review and never ride along in unrelated work. Delivery Every handoff states: changed files, evidence, the validation commands and their results per target on which revision, unresolved findings and the exact review and publication state. "Implemented", "reviewed", "CI passed", "merged" and "published" are different states. Do not keep running diaries of agent activity in the repository; PRs and issues are the record. The files File What to fill in CONTRIBUTING.md OWNER_LOGIN and owner/game ; the section headings stay as in the kit AGENTS.md Nothing in the header; the project's own facts (toolchain, references, style guide, project tools) go under ## Project , never process rules CLAUDE.md Nothing; it imports AGENTS.md .github/pull_request_template.md The target ids in the Targets table README.md Yours, under the seven headings of the kit template: the targets table, the build commands per target, the owner, links to CONTRIBUTING.md and AGENTS.md , the layout table, the credits

title: CI
summary: validate.yml: plan the affected targets, run the tool tests and the scaffold check, build each target in the image, publish on main.
text: CI validate.yml : plan the affected targets, run the tool tests and the scaffold check, build each target in the image, publish on main . One workflow does everything. It runs on every push to main , every pull request and on manual dispatch. Pull requests get the full build and nothing else; pushes to main additionally publish. There is no cache, no artifact and no second workflow to keep in step: the starter validate.yml.template is the whole thing, the four parameters marked in it are the only edits, and one optional step is the only addition. The scaffold check compares the file's job and step names with the kit on every run. Jobs Plan affected targets ──┐ ├──> Validate <target id> (one job per affected active target, in the image) Tool tests ─────────────┘ │ └──> Validate targets (the aggregate check the ruleset requires) Plan affected targets Checks out with fetch-depth: 0 (the planner diffs two commits) and runs python3 tools/ci_targets.py . The planner reads the event: for a pull request it diffs the base SHA against the head, for a push it diffs before against the pushed commit, and for workflow_dispatch , a push without a usable before (first push, force push) or --force-all it selects every active target. It applies config/ci-targets.json ( Targets ), with each target's config/<id>/** and orig/<id>/** derived from the registry, and writes two outputs: matrix : {"include":[{"target":"GAME01-rev0"}, ...]} has_targets : true or false On a pull request the job's second step, Check the declared tier , runs python3 tools/tier.py : it reads the first Tier A , Tier B or Tier C in the PR body and fails when the diff needs more ( config/<id>/splits.txt or symbols.txt , an inferred evidence row, or a cflags , ldflags , asflags or mw_version line in configure.py need A; other source or configure.py changes need B). Outside pull requests it passes. Editing the body does not re-run it; the next push does. The third step, Check the credits , runs python3 tools/credits.py . It does nothing unless config/site.json sets "contributors": true ; then it checks the PR body's Credits: line and every target's credits.tsv and confirms each login exists on GitHub ( Publishing , "Credits"). Nothing finer than selection is attempted. A build-graph planner cannot cover headers without compiler depfiles, so every include/** change selects everything anyway; a target job is about a minute and local builds are incremental through ninja. Tool tests Runs on the plain runner, outside the image, on every event, in two steps: # Run tool tests python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -p 'test_*.py' -v python3 tools/targets.py check python3 tools/versions.py check python3 tools/evidence.py check # Check the scaffold uses: mitsevox/mitsevox.github.io/.github/actions/scaffold-check@main The first step runs the project's tests (add yours under tests/test_*.py ) and the three kit checks: the hashes agree per target, the version blocks use known tokens only, the evidence records are well formed. The second is the scaffold check, a composite action in the site repository. GitHub clones the whole site repository to run it, so the check compares the checkout against the starter kit and the scaffold spec at the action's own revision, and the kit, the spec and the check can never disagree. It prints one ::warning:: per finding and exits 0; with: strict: true makes it fail instead, which the owner flips once every repository has been clean for a month. With the default token it also reads the repository's description, topics, features, merge settings and the rules on main and warns where they differ from the settings standard . Keep anything that needs the toolchain out of this job. Validate <target id> One job per selected target, fail-fast: false , so one target's failure does not cancel another's build or publish. It runs inside the private image, named once at the top of the file. GitHub does not make the env context available to container.image , so the plan job passes the value on as its image output: env: BUILD_IMAGE: ghcr.io/owner/game-build@sha256:<digest> # PARAMETER 1 ... plan: outputs: image: ${{ env.BUILD_IMAGE }} ... permissions: contents: read packages: read pull-requests: read environment: name: ${{ github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && (github.event_name == 'push' || github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch') && 'publish' || 'validate' }} deployment: false container: image: ${{ needs.plan.outputs.image }} credentials: username: ${{ github.actor }} password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} env: TARGET_ID: ${{ matrix.target }} The job references a deployment environment: publish on a push or manual run of main , validate otherwise. publish holds the publishing key as an environment secret and its deployment branch policy allows main only, so a run of any other branch that names publish is refused by GitHub before its first step; validate holds nothing. deployment: false uses the environment's secrets without recording a deployment per run; that the branch policy still applies with it is proven per repository by the two refused probe runs of the move order ( Repository settings , Publishing ). Step What it does Require a repository contribution branch test "$SOURCE_REPOSITORY" = "$GITHUB_REPOSITORY" , where SOURCE_REPOSITORY is the PR head repository or, outside PRs, the repository itself. A fork's PR fails here, before the original is touched. actions/checkout persist-credentials: false ; the default depth is enough because the publish step only needs HEAD . Provide target original mkdir -p orig/$TARGET_ID/sys , cp /orig/$TARGET_ID/sys/main.dol orig/$TARGET_ID/sys/main.dol . PARAMETER 2 is the path. The toolkit checks the hash against config.yml when it splits; a third check of the same bytes is not needed. Configure target python3 configure.py --version "$TARGET_ID" --dtk /usr/local/bin/dtk --binutils /binutils --compilers /compilers . PARAMETER 3. Build, verify complete executable and measure progress ( id: measure ) ninja -f "build/$TARGET_ID/build.ninja" progress "build/$TARGET_ID/report.json" , then writes the output measured-at as the current UTC time in %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ . PARAMETER 3. The build fails unless the executable's hash matches. Check the report uses: mitsevox/mitsevox.github.io/.github/actions/check-report@main with target and report , on every event. It converts the report into the contract files with the same code as the publish step, into an empty tree, and checks them, without a credential and without credits. A report the site would refuse fails the pull request here, not the main publish. A repository that passes code-sections or unit-prefix to the publish step passes the same values here. Project checks , optional The one step a repository may add: its own checks that need the build or the toolchain, with a command of its choice. The template shows it commented out; keep the name. List measuring tools ( id: tools ) Runs python3 tools/measuring_tools.py --verify on every event. The tool reads BUILD_IMAGE from the environment and the tool versions the repository pins (the tags in configure.py , or the JSON pin files its PINS parameter names); --verify runs each command its VERIFY parameter names inside the image ( dtk --version in the kit) and fails the job unless the command exits 0 and the pinned version appears in its output as a whole word ( 1.8.3 is not found in 1.8.30 ), so the provenance published on main names what measured the report, and a pull request that bumps the image digest without the pin, or the pin without the image, fails here. The lines are captured in the output lines with a random heredoc delimiter. Publish to the site , main only uses: mitsevox/mitsevox.github.io/.github/actions/publish@main with target , report: build/<target>/report.json , tools , measured-at , app-client-id and app-private-key . PARAMETER 4 names the repository variable and the publish environment's secret. The publish step and the job's environment use the same condition, github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && (github.event_name == 'push' || github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch') : a push and a manual run on main publish, and nothing else does, the events being named rather than excluded so that an event added later never publishes by accident. Secrets are not available to pull requests from forks anyway, but the fork guard runs first in every case. Validate targets Runs always, after the others, and fails unless plan and tests succeeded and the target jobs either all succeeded (when has_targets was true ) or were skipped (when it was false ). Its name, Validate targets , is the single check the main ruleset requires; the per-target job names vary with the matrix and cannot be required one by one. Workflow-level settings permissions: contents: read concurrency: group: validate-${{ github.ref }} cancel-in-progress: ${{ github.ref != 'refs/heads/main' }} A new push to a PR cancels that PR's running validation; pushes to main queue instead, so every main commit is measured and published. The workflow holds no write permission anywhere; the publish action brings its own credential, read from the publish environment on main runs only. The image is never referenced by tag, and no bot bumps the digest: changing it is a reviewed, owner-decided edit to BUILD_IMAGE . Installing it Copy validate.yml.template to .github/workflows/validate.yml . Fill PARAMETER 1 with the digest from the image workflow ( Build environment ). Fill PARAMETERS 2 and 3 with the original's path and the configure and build commands that work locally ( Build, verify, measure ). The image's tool paths replace the local ones. Fill PARAMETER 4 with the variable and environment secret names from Publishing ; the step is harmless until they exist, because it only runs on main . The owner creates both environments, publish and validate , before the first run. Copy the tools/ and tests/ starter files and config/ci-targets.json . Open a pull request with all of it and watch the four jobs. The first run of Validate <target id> proves the image pull (package access), the original (the toolkit's hash check), the toolchain (configure), the match ( build.sha1 ) and, in Check the report , that the report converts into the site's contract. The Check the scaffold step lists what still differs from the kit. Merge. The first main run publishes, provided the credential is in place. Builds without configure.py A repository whose build is not dtk-template's (its own scripts, a Makefile) keeps the same workflow; only the parameter slots differ: Entry point. build.py or a Makefile at the root (the scaffold accepts either in place of configure.py ). PARAMETER 2. The image still holds /orig/<target id>/sys/main.dol ; the step copies it wherever the build reads it. PARAMETER 3. Configure target runs the build's setup (or true when there is none). Build, verify complete executable and measure progress runs one command that fails unless the complete executable is byte-identical, prints build/<target id>/main.dol: OK (the line every repository's build ends with) and writes an objdiff-shaped build/<target id>/report.json that Check the report accepts (locally: publish.py publish --dry-run --no-credits , Publishing ): measures with total_functions and matched_functions , and units whose sections carry real names and metadata.virtual_address . The code-sections and unit-prefix the report needs go to both the report check and the publish step. Measuring tools. Set PINS in tools/measuring_tools.py to the JSON files that pin the tools ( {"<name>": {"version": ...}} ), and VERIFY to the command that prints each image-installed tool's version, so that --verify confirms those pins against the image. List every tool whose --version prints the pinned version as a whole word and exits 0; a tool whose pin is not what it prints (binutils pinned as 2.42-2 prints 2.42 ) cannot be listed, and only the version word is verified, never anything a pin says after it, such as a local patch's hash. Tools. Every tool the build runs is baked into the build image, as in the kit's Dockerfile; the target job downloads nothing. Tool tests. The Tool tests job runs on the bare runner; a test that needs the toolchain skips there and runs in Project checks instead. Build inputs. tests/** is a nonBuild pattern in the kit because every test runs in Tool tests . A repository whose tests run in Project checks moves tests/** from nonBuild to shared in config/ci-targets.json , so that a test change rebuilds every target where that test runs ( Targets ). What a pull request proves A green Validate targets on a PR means: the tool tests pass, and for every target the change can affect, the complete executable built from the PR's source plus the original bytes for unlinked ranges is byte-identical to the original, objdiff produced a report, and that report converts into the site's contract. It does not mean the reconstruction is right; that is what the review tiers in Contribution workflow are for. Pull requests publish nothing, so a PR cannot change the site.

title: Publishing
summary: The GitHub App credential, the publish action's inputs and what happens on a push to main.
text: Publishing The GitHub App credential, the publish action's inputs and what happens on a push to main . Publishing is one step at the end of each Validate <target id> job on main . The step is the composite action mitsevox/mitsevox.github.io/.github/actions/publish , referenced at @main . It converts the objdiff report into the contract files, validates them, and pushes them to the data repository with a short-lived token minted from a GitHub App. The producer holds the App's client id and private key; the site holds nothing. The credential The credential is a GitHub App installed on the data repository only, with Contents: read and write as its only repository permission (plus the mandatory Metadata: read ). It is not installed on the producer. The action mints a one-hour installation token scoped to the data repository at the start of the step; the token is revoked when the job ends. For the owner's site the App already exists and is installed on mitsevox/decomp-data ; a new game needs its client id and private key as a variable and a secret in the producer repository. For a new data repository, create the App once: GitHub Settings, Developer settings, GitHub Apps, New GitHub App ( documentation ). Any name; no webhook; Where can this GitHub App be installed? Only on this account. Repository permissions: Contents: Read and write . Leave every other permission at no access. Never add Actions or Workflows. After creating it, note the Client ID on the App's page and generate a private key (a .pem file downloads). Install the App on the account, choosing Only select repositories and selecting the data repository alone. Then, in the producer repository: Kind Where Name used in this guide Value Repository variable Settings, Secrets and variables, Actions, Variables DATA_APP_CLIENT_ID The App's client id Environment secret Settings, Environments, publish , Environment secrets DATA_APP_PRIVATE_KEY The full contents of the .pem file The names are yours; validate.yml passes them to the action as app-client-id: ${{ vars.DATA_APP_CLIENT_ID }} and app-private-key: ${{ secrets.DATA_APP_PRIVATE_KEY }} (PARAMETER 4). The private key is an environment secret and never a repository secret, because a repository secret is readable by a workflow run of any branch of the repository, and contributors push branches. The publish environment's deployment branch policy allows main only. The target job references publish on a push or manual run of main and the empty environment validate on every other run, so a run of any other branch, including one that edits validate.yml to name publish , is refused by GitHub before its first step ( CI ). The owner creates the environments once: Settings, Environments, New environment, name publish , Configure environment. Deployment branches and tags: choose "Selected branches and tags", Add deployment branch or tag rule, ref type Branch, name pattern main , Add rule. No tag rule: a tag rule would let any contributor's tag push reach the key. Environment secrets, Add environment secret: name DATA_APP_PRIVATE_KEY , value the .pem contents. Leave required reviewers and the wait timer off. New environment, name validate , Configure environment, change nothing: every branch, no secrets. Both environments are created by hand (or by python3 tools/repo_settings.py --apply ), never left to appear on their own: GitHub documents that a referenced environment is created on the fly, but does not say whether this happens for a job with deployment: false . The settings standard checks both ( Repository settings ). A repository secret and an environment secret may share a name. A job that references an environment reads the environment's secret when the environment has one of that name, and otherwise falls back to the repository secret. So the key must not exist as a repository secret at all once the environment holds it, and the move from one to the other follows the order in Repository settings , which deletes the repository secret before trusting a published line and then proves the branch policy with two refused runs.
